facts.fact: Helix: outer posterosuperior rim of the ear, curving slightly inward toward the external acoustic meatus (definition from search-result summary; not verified against full text).
Antihelix: Y-shaped ridge arising from the antitragus that separates the concha, triangular fossa and scapha; its upper arms are the crura, bounding the deep conchal bowl.

Concha is the hollow next to the ear canal, bounded by the tragus, intertragal notch, antitragus, antihelix, inferior crus of the antihelix and root of the helix; the external auditory meatus opens into it.

Tragus is a cartilaginous projection anterior to the ear canal that partially occludes the meatus; antitragus is the opposing smaller protrusion forming the inferior concha boundary and posterior wall of the intertragal notch.
Lobule (earlobe) is the inferior extremity of the auricle, soft and fleshy with no cartilaginous framework.
North India mixed adults: mean auricle length 6.28 cm (right) and 6.23 cm (left); mean width 3.21 cm (right) and 3.28 cm (left). Males had greater total auricle height and width than females.

Sundanese (West Java) photogrammetry: men auricle length 6.29 cm (SD 0.47), width 2.95 cm (SD 0.26); women length 6.09 cm (SD 0.42), width 2.88 cm (SD 0.25). The women's concha width value in the abstract (0.42 cm) appears to be a typo per the summary.
Mixed adult sample (n=200): ear length 57.62 ± 5.03 mm right and 57.89 ± 4.89 mm left; ear breadth 29.72 ± 2.79 mm right and 31.21 ± 2.95 mm left.
Across a review of studies aged roughly 17-30, male auricle height spans about 59.5 to 68.5 mm and male width shows about a 12 mm range between studies.

Length definitions differ: one review measures auricle length from most superior to most inferior projection; the Sundanese study measures superaurale to subaurale. Norms must be compared using the same landmarks and units.

Protrusion criteria (2011, n=44 patients): ear considered prominent if upper protrusion exceeds 21.5 mm or lower exceeds 20.0 mm in boys; upper >17.5 mm or lower >15.5 mm in girls. The study argues different criteria should be used for boys and girls.
The same 2011 study suggests the common otoplasty success criterion of asymmetry under 3 mm may be too strict.

Auriculocephalic (protrusion) angle: one StatPearls-style summary gives a normal range of roughly 20-30 degrees between skull and helix; another source says the auricle normally projects no more than 2 cm from the mastoid, forming an angle under 25 degrees. The two norms differ slightly.

Molded-ear study (small sample, illustrative): mean cephaloauricular angle 47.7 degrees in study group vs 31.1 degrees in controls; scaphaconchal angle 132.6 vs 106.7 degrees. Source URL for these figures was not confirmed.
Different studies have measured ear protrusion, long-axis inclination and ear level with different methods, so the reported data are hard to compare across studies.
A 3D study defines the auriculocephalic angle as the angle between plane normals fit to the mastoid and auricle surfaces, a different method from ruler or photo measurement.

Sex differences: males show significantly greater ear length and width than females in a Central Indian adult sample (p=0.0001 both sides), and in a Saudi pediatric sample; lobule measures were also larger in males in the pediatric study.
Width is inconsistent by sex: an Eastern Saudi adult study found no significant male-female difference in right ear width, with similar results reported in a Turkish population.
Lobule height and lobule index often show no significant sex difference; absolute length and width have greater discriminatory power for sex than proportional indices (one study).
Chinese growth study: ear length reached mature size by age 14 in both males and females, with gender and ethnic differences in development.
Ear shape classified as round, oval, rectangular or triangular in a Central Indian population; shape was judged less useful for sex determination than metric parameters.
Forensic ear comparison has been used for about 40 years; an early system used twelve ear measurements. The earlobe is the ear part most often examined in forensic cases (per one source).

Ear shape claimed stable: one source says full development by the fourth month after birth with later growth only in size; another says size and shape hold steady until about age 70. Significant shape change is reported between about 4 months and 8 years. These are secondary-source claims, not verified against primary papers.

Combined ear and face biometrics achieved a 97.1% recognition rate in a border-control setting (one cited study); ear recognition rates are usually over 90% and fall to about 80% or lower as imaging angle changes (one review).
Ear tissue is elastic and can be deliberately deformed to defeat ear recognition systems.

contradictions: Auriculocephalic angle norms: 20-30 degrees (StatPearls-style summary) vs under 25 degrees with projection of 2 cm or less from the mastoid (second source).
Ear width sex difference: significant in Central Indian and Saudi pediatric samples, not significant in Eastern Saudi adults and similar Turkish results.
Sundanese women's concha width value (0.42 cm) in the abstract looks inconsistent with the rest of the data; treat as a likely typo.
Units differ across sources (cm vs mm) and length definitions differ (superior-inferior projection vs superaurale-subaurale), so direct numeric comparison is unreliable.
Source URLs for several numbers (molded-ear angles, 3D plane-normal angle, shape-stability claims) were not reliably mapped to a URL in the results.
